I have three Siberian Huskies that are VORACIOUS Chicken/Rawhide eaters. Of all the treats I have ever come across, its the Chicken wrapped rawhide that is their absolute favorite. Several different companies offer them, but I am always on the lookout for a new offering. Came across "A Heart for Paws" from Black Mountain Supply on my last Amazon search and since they were all natural and coming from my home state of Idaho, I ordered a package for testing. Well, I am here to say my 3 huskies LOVED THEM. They powered through a package of them in no time at all.
The only negative thing I would say is that I wish they offered this in a BIGGER version. Huskies generally run in the 35-50lb range, and I would say these treats are on the smallish side for a dog that size. They were easily able to CRUNCH right through the entire stick in a couple minutes, rather than having to CHEW/GNAW there way through the rawhide. NOT a fault of the manufacturer, just need a BIGGER sized option. But the Doggoes LOVED THEM and I will get more of them.

Forget your old metallic press you have, THIS is worth every dollar I spent on it.

First of the aesthetics: This thing is drop dead beautiful and you'd be proud to leave it out like a nice accessory because its that pretty! The pictures do not do it justice.

Construction/craftsmanship: Gosh, where do I start. Its a night and day difference from my old metallic one I got in Mexico decades ago. The construction/craftsmanship is perfect. Silky smooth woods, food grade oil finish, just wonderful.

Function: If you can use the old press, the learning curve is nil here. Just use the quart ziploc bag (cut off the zip top, split the bag on the sides and dont cut the bottom) and there's no cleaning issues. Unlike a metallic one you just dont mash down on it. Constant pressure and hold for a few seconds to get the full size of the tortilla. Open up peel from the zip lock and comal time!

What could be better: Three things. 1. Silicone/no slip feets would have been nice. Since the wood is oiled now, it will be hard to stick and I really don't want to drill into it to put rubber feet on it. So I have a silicone trivet under it. Fixes that. 2. The bolt/hinge. I don't know. To be honest it does take away from it. It works but it doesn't look as good as it should. I hope the craftsman reads this. An idea would be to cut a 1/4 stainless rod, tap it through to within a 1/4" each side then tap in wooded plugs like the rest of the screw parts. And last one. The hinges. They work. looks good. But, would wooded hinges hold out? Probably would add to the cost due to the work involved with the jigs and stuff but oh would it look pretty. Eh...They work.

Other than that, You see 70 bucks for a tortilla press and ask is it worth it when my La Victoria is just as good. No, its not just as good. Its much better! Like a black-n-decker blender vs a kitchenaid. Yeah they both make cake batter but Its not as sexy. And if you cry hard enough to the S.O...GET IT. You wont be sorry.

As a self-proclaimed Kitchen Diva, I absolutely had to get this apron. Now wearing it makes me laugh so hard that I can’t even cry while I'm chopping onions.

Aside from the catchy slogan, here are some of the other positive things about the apron. It’s quite long, extending down below my knees (I’m 5’ 6”). I appreciate the fact the neck strap has an easily adjustable plastic slider rather than interlocking D-rings – those tend to be a pain to use, and often don’t stay in place. The two front pockets are deep, and are seemingly well stitched, as are the other seams on the apron.

There are a few things that could be better or that give me pause, resulting in a 4-star review rather than 5-stars.

First, I wish the ties were a bit longer. They’re fine if you choose to tie the apron in back, but they’re a bit too short to be able to comfortably wrap completely around to tie a front bow.

Next, the product description says the apron is made from “heavy-duty thick polyester” and some folks have described it as being like “canvas.” Ummm, my apron doesn’t fit either of those descriptions since the material mine is made from is actually rather thin. If I hold the apron up to a window, I can see light shadows and outlines of objects through it. I wish the material was thicker, more consistent with standard kitchen aprons.

There’s a place on the inside of the apron where it appears the fabric label or care instructions were torn out. In the product description online it states, “It's easy to wash and use of dryer, spin-dry or dry-clean is not recommended.” Frankly, that’s rather confusing. On one hand it seems to way it’s fine to wash it and use the dryer, but on the other hand it seems to say spin-dry is not advised. Is this a glitch with punctuation or grammar in the copy? Maybe the intention was to say, “It’s easy to wash, BUT use of dryer, spin-dry or dry-clean is not recommended.” Who knows? At this point, I sure don't.

Speaking of washing, I wonder how many wash cycles the catchy white applique will survive. Product details describe the apron as having an “embroidered design.” Nope! It’s definitely just printed on the fabric – not embroidered.

Folks, this is a kitchen apron. If it’s actually going to be used while cooking, it DEFINITELY WILL get dirty. The cleaning instructions need to be clear – and they need to be included on a tag with the apron, especially since this item seems like one that will be given as a gift.

The two-sentence version of this review:
I bought this sleeve almost exactly 1 year ago for my 2017 15" MacBook Pro and it is still safely, beautifully, and perfectly protecting my laptop.

If you want thorough PROS, CONS, and OTHER THOUGHTS though, please read on.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

So, I'm the kind of consumer who:
1) loves details (so be prepared for a long review)
2) reads as many reviews as possible prior to purchase (ex. 5-6 hours of reading up on phone cases for my iPhone 7 plus)
3) will spend more for quality on something I'm going to constantly use 9 out of 10 times because I value stewarding what I am given well
Be prepared for all this.

PREFACE:
So, flashback to Sep 17, 2017, I was using a cheap Tomtoc sleeve to handle my new laptop—a 2017 15" Touch Bar MacBook Pro—while I was looking for a better option.
Which, on that note, don't get one if you've got this same laptop. It's useless as it's far too roomy, allowing the laptop to haphazardly shift around all the time. (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01H4ZRJ9I/ref=oh_aui_search_detailpage?ie=UTF8&psc=1)

Anyways, I had spent 10+ hours reviewing mass-produced cases on Amazon, pricey handmade Etsy ones, etc. and was starting to give up on my search. In my frustration, I decided I was going to be cheap and settle on a solid $40-50 case.
There was one brand that stood out to me and was constantly mentioned in reviews everywhere: Picaso Lab.

I did really love my my best bud's Picaso Lab sleeve that he'd had for years. Whenever I handled it it felt great to the touch and fit his MacBook Pro like a glove. After learning that I was temporarily using that cheap one, my friend rebuked and convinced me I too should get a Picaso Lab with one question:

You're not willing to spend $100 to protect your $2,400 laptop?

Bam. Right there. I pulled open Amazon Smile and bought mine (USE SMILE IF YOU AREN'T ALREADY! You'll be supporting charities and NGOs through your normal Amazon usage).

Now that I've used my Picaso Lab sleeve for a year, here are some comprehensive thoughts.
I'll start off with the short list of negatives and then segue into its wonderful positives.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

CONS:

1) EXPENSIVE
I'm not going to pretend it's not a lot of $; it is. This sleeve is a LUXURY. Also, a $2,400 laptop is a LUXURY. I could have spent that $100 and sponsored an underprivileged child's education for several months (World Vision - https://www.worldvision.org/sponsor-a-child). $2,400 would cover 1/6 the cost of providing clean, safe water and sanitation for a WHOLE community of hundreds if not thousands in Africa (The Water Project - https://thewaterproject.org/give-water).

So, PLEASE DON'T SPEND $ ON THIS if you think it could be of better use elsewhere for others. I encourage you to reconsider your financial decisions and be more selfless because most of us ought to.

However, I know my laptop and sleeve are going to be used to give back more than they cost thus I'd gladly make this purchase all over again. I am committed to serving and giving to those near and far because that's what Jesus would do and what we all should do. So, I know this sleeve is an investment to protect the effective tool that I use to bless others called a laptop.

2) IT'S A LITTLE LOOSE NOW
This might be me nitpicking, but I wish that my sleeve stayed as tight on my laptop as it did when I first received it.
If you look at Picture #3, you can see that there's a slight gap when my laptop is placed in my Picaso Lab. That gap wasn't there the first several months of use, but I've definitely put a ton of figurative and literal miles on this (more on that later in PRO point #1).

At first, I could put the MacBook Pro in the sleeve, hold it upside down, and vigorously shake it for 30 seconds and barely anything. All this would cause it to peak out just the tiniest bit. However, now I'll just hold it upside down and jiggle it side to side and it's what you see in Picture #2.

This isn't my ideal, but how often is someone sane going to hold an open-ended sleeve like that for a prolonged period of time? It's a bit of a bummer, but I'm grateful that this is such a negligible negative.

3) I WISH THERE WAS A CLASP OF SOME SORT

Yeah. I wish there was a strap thingamajig that kept the laptop from just-in-case falling out. See above con though and once again, negligible negative. Now onto all the things I really love about the Picaso Lab.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

THE SWEET PROS:

1) DURABILITY, DURABILITY, DURABILITY!
If there's a reason to buy a laptop sleeve or a $1,500 iPhone Xwhatever case or anything that is supposed to shield your pricey tech gear from the harsh, bitter world around it's this. I have no idea why anyone would buy something that looks great but does a crappy job at actually protecting their incredibly expensive investment. That's just vanity.
My black leather, red thread Picaso Lab sleeve is a BOSS though at keeping my MacBook Pro MINT.

After getting shoved into my backpack all the time, accidentally dropping it at short heights at least once (3-4 ft off carpeted ground), lugged around all over the West Coast then used in both hot and cold weather, and traveling with me halfway across the world and back this summer, my laptop has no visible or felt nicks or scratches. It is in actual perfect visible condition. It also serves as a good buffer between my laptop and any questionable surfaces underneath.

It's not a hard case, which would be the ultimate step-up for laptop protection, but the Picaso Lab is the next best thing. It has TOUGH EDGES AND CORNERS that have no give when I bump it on things and somehow simultaneously is SOFT to my laptop. However, I know the only thing that's ultimately keeping my MacBook Pro safe is my Picaso Lab sleeve. When it's in my backpack or I'm holding it under my arm, I am fully confident nothing is going to harm my laptop barring some freak accident like a biker barreling into me.

The leather feels great and like any well-treated leather, it smells fantastic, too.

I have no idea how old the Alex gentleman who makes these is, but for as long as he is alive he is a blessing to MacBook owners everywhere. Why? He has a LIFETIME WARRANTY attached to this stupendous product.

Alex is the real stuff and you should also do business with him if you're wanting something custom. One more reason to buy a Picaso Lab, right? Now onto my final point and it only makes sense if you believe in the U.S.A..

5) SUPPORTING SKILLED, MADE IN THE U.S.A. LABOR
A worker is worth their wages and someone who does such a great job providing incredible products is definitely worth what they're selling. No matter where the product is coming from or what its creators background is, if something is excellent it is valuable and it deserves a price accordingly paid.
However, as a citizen of the United States of America, I believe in free enterprise that also invests into as much local economy as possible. Money has an exponential effect around us when its sown into the local economy. Financial advice aside, I myself am a Californian and when I read that Alex lives and makes these in California, it was a no-brainer cherry on top of my purchase.
I'm not being a patriot for patriotism's sake. I do believe though that the U.S.A, for all its faults, is the most privileged and free country in the world and provides the greatest opportunity for people to do good of any place in the world.

Today, I got my 7 wk old adodpted pup to the first stage of ringing bell. In preparation to getting him to ring bell when he needs to go out. He was doing fair with it. I have a different brand of chicken jerky. I didn't like it 100%. It is imported and has preservatives. I have doubts because the label puts a daily limit on amount to feed dog. I am of the school that treats are treats. The only real limit is calorie and nutritional intake based on dog. Also the jerky is in strips that are hard to break in small enough portions for my pup. I got these and was impressed with packaging. The amount was broken down into 3 sealed packages. 2 went into freezer. #3 was opened. It smelled so good that I honestly had to stop myself from taking 'just a little taste'! The cats were there sniffing along with the pup. These are the perfect size for a pup (or cat) treat. They are perfect for any dog training. Dogs prefer frequent small treats vs rare large treats. As said earlier, my pup is at stage 1 bell ringing. In theory, I say 'bell', he rings it, I gave a bit of the other chicken jerky treat. After he got a taste of this, he ran to bell. Then proceeded to train me. He rang bell, I give a treat. The only way I stopped him was to put him in his sleeping area. Made me feel kinda guilty. Updated 03Nov2017. The mini bites make pup/dog training so much easier. The key to reward for doing something is immediate reward, praise. The key to reward is for treat to be large enough for a taste but small enough to be eaten in a few chews. My pup is (currently) small. I break the mini bites smaller. In a few short weeks he has learned his name, outside facility usage (now nearly 100%), sit, come, stay (only 5 minutes), kennel (his private area), tub (yes, bath tub for those future baths), paw (not shake, this is for nail trims) and more. I keep a zip lock bag with treats in them at strategic places. The treats came subdivided into 5 or 6 ounce sealed bags. I am liberal with treats. I decrease the frequency as needed. His name,, outside facility usage, sit, tub, and kennel now only get treats a few times a day. Other things or new I treat as indicated. A 5 ounce bag, with me breaking treats smaller as needed, lasts about 8 days. This makes these treats an excellent investment. Since it has been so long since I had a pup, I looked at various on line training videos. The vast majority of trainers gave treats of some sort. One individual gave cooked chicken breast chunks. Well these are far easier for me then cooking and chopping the chicken.
